prompt: In the first run against lesson 4's environment, Create order answered 401 although the pre-request script had fetched a token. Why?
hint: Which scope is narrower?

choices.text: The pre-request script fetched the token too late, after the request had left
choices.why: Pre-request scripts finish before the variables are resolved and the request is sent.

choices.text: The environment's empty token hid the collection's
choices.why: Right. The environment is narrower, and an empty value still wins.

choices.text: boxoffice refuses a token fetched by a script
choices.why: boxoffice cannot tell how a token was fetched; it checks the signature and the expiry.

choices.text: The token had expired between the two requests
choices.why: They were milliseconds apart, and a token lives 15 minutes.

prompt: A run shows ten failures. The first is a 401 on Create order; the rest mention 8080null. Where should you start?
hint: Which failures are echoes?

choices.text: With the RangeError, because it is the strangest message
choices.why: Strange is not first; the RangeError comes from an orderUrl that the 401 left empty.

choices.text: With the last failure, which sums up the others
choices.why: Newman lists failures in the order they happened; the last one sums nothing up.

choices.text: With the 401
choices.why: Right. The others follow from it: no location, so no orderUrl.

choices.text: With Newman's port setting, which must be wrong
choices.why: The port is fine; the address was built from null.

prompt: In the whole run with the fixed environment, how many assertions passed?
hint: Executed minus failed, in the assertions row.

prompt: What makes a pm.test fail?
hint: A test is a name and a function.

choices.text: Its function throws an error
choices.why: Right. A failed assertion throws, and so does any other error inside it.

choices.text: Its function returns false
choices.why: A return value is ignored; only a thrown error fails it.

choices.text: The response status is 400 or above
choices.why: A test of a 404 can pass; the status matters only if a test checks it.

choices.text: Its name does not match the request's name
choices.why: The name is a label for the report.

prompt: Which assertion passes when the response body is {"seats":1,"status":"confirmed"}?
hint: Same value or same contents?

choices.text: pm.expect(pm.response.json()).to.equal({seats: 1, status: 'confirmed'})
choices.why: equal asks whether they are the same object, and two objects that look alike are not.

choices.text: pm.expect(pm.response.json()).to.eql({seats: 1, status: 'confirmed'})
choices.why: Right. eql compares contents, field by field.

choices.text: pm.expect(pm.response.json().seats).to.equal('1')
choices.why: The body holds the number 1, not the string '1'.

choices.text: pm.expect(pm.response.json()).to.have.lengthOf(2)
choices.why: An object has no length; lengthOf is for arrays and strings.

prompt: Why is pm.expect(pm.response.code === 200).to.be.true a poor assertion?
hint: Read what it says when it fails.

choices.text: It never fails, because === always returns true
choices.why: It fails on any other code; the trouble is what it says then.

choices.text: pm.response.code does not exist in Postman
choices.why: It exists: it is the status as a number.

choices.text: Chai cannot compare booleans
choices.why: It can; to.be.true is a Chai assertion.

choices.text: Its failure says expected false to be true and nothing about the status
choices.why: Right. Asserting on the value lets Chai say which status came back.

prompt: Match each object to what it is.
hint: The table in the section.

pairs.right: a named check that fails when fn throws

right_distractors: the request about to be sent

prompt: Why do Read order and Cancel order use {{baseUrl}}{{orderUrl}} instead of a fixed order id?
hint: Which order should they act on?

choices.text: boxoffice refuses a request that spells out the order id
choices.why: boxoffice answers /v1/orders/ord-1001 like any other path; the path is the same either way.

choices.text: So they reach this run's order
choices.why: Right. location says where the order this run created lives, whatever its number.

choices.text: Because location is faster to read than the body
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; the order's identity is.

choices.text: Because collection variables cannot hold an id
choices.why: They hold any string, an id included.

prompt: A teammate changes the Get token script to save the token with pm.environment.set instead. In a team that shares the environment, what is the trouble?
hint: Who else reads the environment?

choices.text: Postman forbids scripts from writing to an environment
choices.why: pm.environment.set exists and works.

choices.text: The token would be sent twice in every request
choices.why: A variable resolves to one value; it is sent once.

choices.text: None at all, since environment and collection are the same scope
choices.why: They are two scopes, and the environment is the narrower.

choices.text: A run writes into shared configuration, so other people's values change
choices.why: Right. The token belongs to one run, which is the collection's business.

prompt: Create order saves the new order's address from the response header called ___.
hint: A 201 carries it.

prompt: Why does the collection make a new Idempotency-Key before each order instead of writing one fixed key in the header?
hint: What does boxoffice do with a key it has seen?

choices.text: boxoffice refuses any request without a new random key
choices.why: The key is optional; boxoffice takes orders without one.

choices.text: A reused key replays the first order
choices.why: Right. The first run's order comes back, and every test would pass with no new order made.

choices.text: A fixed key would reveal the client secret
choices.why: The key is a random identifier and carries no credentials.

choices.text: Postman cannot send the same header value twice
choices.why: It sends whatever the header says, as often as asked.

prompt: Put what happens for the Create order request in order.
hint: Variables are resolved after every pre-request script.
items: the request's pre-request script sets idempotencyKey
the variables in the request are resolved

prompt: Why is thirty seconds taken off expires_in when tokenExpires is saved?
hint: A request takes time to travel.

choices.text: boxoffice's clock runs thirty seconds fast
choices.why: Nothing says so; the margin is about requests in flight.

choices.text: expires_in counts in units of thirty seconds
choices.why: expires_in is in seconds; 900 is fifteen minutes.

choices.text: A token that expires on its way is refused
choices.why: Right. The margin costs one extra token request now and then.

choices.text: Postman needs thirty seconds to save a variable
choices.why: Saving a variable is immediate.

prompt: The seat rules folder also runs in a whole-collection run with no data file. Which values does Order seats use then?
hint: Who else defines seats and expected?

choices.text: None: the request is skipped without a data file
choices.why: It ran: section 02's run ends with Order seats.

choices.text: The values of the last data file used
choices.why: Newman keeps nothing from one run to the next.

choices.text: The literal text {{seats}}, so the request fails with 400
choices.why: seats is defined in the collection, so it resolves.

choices.text: The collection's defaults, 1 and 201
choices.why: Right. With a file, the data scope is narrower and wins.

prompt: The data run made one more request than it had iterations. How many requests did it make?
hint: The requests row of the table.

prompt: A colleague proposes adding rows for 2, 3, 4 and 5 seats to seats.csv. What does the section say about that?
hint: Every row is a claim.

choices.text: More rows always make the run more thorough
choices.why: Rows inside one class add runs, not information.

choices.text: They sit between the boundaries already there and test nothing new
choices.why: Right. 1 and 6 already stand for the valid class.

choices.text: Newman accepts at most six rows per file
choices.why: There is no such limit; the point is what the rows test.

choices.text: They would sell out sh-101 and fail
choices.why: sh-101 has 120 seats; four more orders would not empty it.

prompt: The brittle collection passed on its first run and failed on its second. What changed in between?
hint: Read the second run's failure.

choices.text: boxoffice started answering orders with a different status
choices.why: Both runs got 201 Created.

choices.text: The token from the first run expired
choices.why: Each run fetched its own token, and both orders were created.

choices.text: Only the order's number, ord-1002
choices.why: Right. The API did nothing wrong; the test asserted an id it was never promised.

choices.text: The data file was missing
choices.why: The brittle collection uses no data file.

prompt: Which of these are safe for a test of Create order to assert?
hint: What did the API promise?

choices.text: The status is 201
choices.why: Right: the code is part of the contract.

choices.text: The id matches /^ord-\d+$/
choices.why: Right: the shape, not the number.

choices.text: The id is ord-1001
choices.why: That depends on what ran before.

choices.text: The Date header contains today's date as written in the test
choices.why: That depends on the clock.

choices.text: seats is the number that was sent
choices.why: Right: it is what the request asked for.

prompt: Why is asserting the whole body of an order with eql a poor test even on a freshly started boxoffice?
hint: Think of the day boxoffice changes harmlessly.

choices.text: It fails when a harmless field is added
choices.why: Right. Assert the fields the test is about.

choices.text: eql cannot compare nested objects
choices.why: eql compares nested objects field by field.

choices.text: Comparing a whole body is too slow for a test
choices.why: It takes microseconds; speed is not the trouble.

choices.text: It passes even when the order is wrong
choices.why: It fails on any difference, which is the trouble.

prompt: In Postman you run only the orders folder at 14:00, after Get token ran at 13:30. Which part of the collection keeps Create order from answering 401?
hint: The token lives 15 minutes.

choices.text: The bearer setting on the collection
choices.why: It sends {{token}} as it is, expired or not.

choices.text: Get token's test script
choices.why: Get token is in the auth folder, which this run leaves out.

choices.text: The collection's pre-request script
choices.why: Right. It sees tokenExpires has passed and fetches a new token.

choices.text: The Idempotency-Key header
choices.why: The key prevents a double order; it is not a credential.

prompt: You add a test to Read order asserting pm.response.json().id equals 'ord-1001'. The whole collection passes on your machine and fails in a colleague's run. Which explanation fits?
hint: Did the colleague's boxoffice have orders already?

choices.text: The colleague's Newman is a different version
choices.why: Both ran 6.2.3, the version npx was told to fetch.

choices.text: Their boxoffice already had orders
choices.why: Right. So this run's order got a later number. The id depends on what ran before; compare it with orderUrl instead.

choices.text: orderUrl is shared between the two machines
choices.why: Collection variables live in each run; nothing is shared.

choices.text: Their environment defines token as empty
choices.why: Then Create order would answer 401 and Read order would never be built from a valid orderUrl.

prompt: boxoffice is fixed and HEAD now answers 200. What happens to the collection's run, and what should you do with the HEAD test?
hint: A failing test was the defect report.

choices.text: The run still fails, because HEAD carries no body to parse
choices.why: The HEAD test checks only the status.

choices.text: The run passes, and the HEAD test should be deleted as done
choices.why: Deleting it removes the guard against the defect coming back.

choices.text: The run passes; keep the test, which now guards against a regression
choices.why: Right. It turned green without anybody remembering to check.

choices.text: The run passes only after the test is changed to expect 405
choices.why: 405 was the defect; 200 is what the test always expected.
